items.title: NASA-JAXA XRISM Mission Sees Pulsar Gathering Companion's 'Wind'
items.hook: A pulsar caught feeding on its companion's wind
items.body: The XRISM X-ray observatory watched stellar wind streaming off a giant star and being captured by the neutron star orbiting it. The plasma falls toward the pulsar at roughly 335,000 mph. Wind-fed accretion had been inferred before, but not resolved directly like this.
items.why: It's the first direct look at the mechanism that powers a whole class of X-ray binaries.

jargon.accretion: matter falling onto a dense object

points: XRISM watched a neutron star capturing a giant star's wind.
Plasma falls toward the pulsar at roughly 335,000 mph.
First direct look at what powers a class of X-ray binaries.

items.title: FLEX and Sentinel-3C launch highlights
items.hook: FLEX launched to watch plants glow
items.body: ESA's FLEX Earth Explorer and Copernicus Sentinel-3C went up together on a Vega-C from French Guiana on 15 September — the rocket's first dual launch using the Vespa adapter. FLEX measures the faint fluorescence plants emit while photosynthesising; Sentinel-3C continues ocean, land, ice and atmosphere monitoring.
items.why: Plant fluorescence is a direct readout of photosynthesis happening, not a proxy for it.
points: ESA launched FLEX and Sentinel-3C together on one Vega-C.
Rocket's first dual launch, using the Vespa adapter, on 15 September.
FLEX reads plant fluorescence, a direct measure of photosynthesis.

items.title: Galileo's first civil authenticated position fix under spoofing conditions
items.hook: Galileo held its position fix while being spoofed
items.body: On 16 September five operational Galileo satellites broadcast a new encrypted test signal. Receivers in Norway and at ESA's ESTEC established their location from it — the first real-world positioning using Galileo's upcoming Signal Authentication Service, under deliberate spoofing conditions.
items.why: Civil GNSS spoofing is now routine near conflict zones; authentication is the defence.
points: Galileo receivers fixed their position despite deliberate spoofing.
Five satellites broadcast a new encrypted Signal Authentication test signal.
Authentication defends against spoofing now routine near conflict zones.

items.body: NASA extended SpaceX's Commercial Crew contract with Crew-15, Crew-16 and Crew-17, readiness dates in 2027 and 2028. The modification is worth $946 million and brings SpaceX's total to 17 missions.

jargon.readiness date: when the flight can first launch

Worth $946 million, bringing SpaceX to 17 missions through 2028.
Shapes how the station stays crewed late in its life.

items.title: COSI Telescope Comes Together
items.hook: COSI's gamma-ray detector is assembled
items.body: Engineers at UC Berkeley put together the detector for COSI, the Compton Spectrometer and Imager, in July 2026. The telescope is built to study energetic cosmic phenomena including matter–antimatter annihilation and stellar evolution, with UC San Diego and the Naval Research Laboratory among the partners.
items.why: Gamma-ray lines from annihilating positrons are one of the few direct traces of antimatter in the galaxy.

jargon.Compton imaging: reconstructing gamma rays from scatter angles

points: UC Berkeley engineers assembled the COSI gamma-ray telescope's detector.
Built in July 2026 with UC San Diego and Naval Research Laboratory.
Could trace antimatter in the galaxy via positron annihilation lines.

items.title: ESA starts next phase of IRIS² evolution through Low-LEO activities
items.hook: 80 companies, 18 contracts, one European constellation
items.body: ESA signed 18 consolidation contracts drawing in nearly 80 companies to study secure, resilient connectivity services for the EU's IRIS² constellation, with a focus on very low Earth orbit.
items.why: IRIS² is Europe's answer to depending on non-European satellite communications.

jargon.Low-LEO: orbits below the usual LEO band

points: ESA signed 18 contracts for the EU's IRIS² constellation.
Nearly 80 companies will study services, focusing on very low orbit.
Aims to cut Europe's reliance on non-European satellite communications.

items.title: Constraints on the Higgs boson total width from on-shell signal-background interference in the H→γγ decay channel
items.hook: Higgs width pinned below 307 MeV
items.body: The Higgs boson's natural width is far too narrow to measure directly. ATLAS instead used the interference between the resonant Higgs signal and the continuum background in the two-photon channel, setting an observed upper limit of 307 MeV (258 MeV expected) at 95% confidence.
items.why: The width is where undiscovered particles would show up first — anything the Higgs decays into invisibly widens it.
points: ATLAS set a new upper limit on the Higgs boson's width.
Observed limit 307 MeV at 95% confidence, via two-photon interference.
Invisible decays to undiscovered particles would widen the Higgs first.

items.title: A heterogeneous and vectorized sequence for the HL-LHC full tracking reconstruction of the CMS experiment
authors: Emmanouil Vourliotis (on behalf of CMS Collaboration)
items.hook: CMS rebuilds its track reconstruction for HL-LHC
items.body: The High-Luminosity LHC will pile far more simultaneous collisions into each event than the current tracking software was built for. CMS's Phase-2 strategy splits the work between GPU-optimised algorithms and vectorised CPU code to keep reconstruction tractable.
items.why: At HL-LHC rates, physics reach is limited by what the reconstruction can keep up with, not by the detector.
points: CMS redesigned its track reconstruction for the High-Luminosity LHC.
Splits work between GPU-optimised algorithms and vectorised CPU code.
Reconstruction speed, not the detector, will limit HL-LHC physics reach.

items.title: OSIRIS-REx Returned a Pristine Sample of Asteroid Bennu
items.hook: Bennu's 121.6 g came back almost perfectly clean
items.body: OSIRIS-REx returned 121.6 grams of regolith from asteroid Bennu in 2023. A 69-author contamination audit tracked every way spacecraft materials could have tainted the sample, and concludes it meets the formal definition of pristine — except for one isolated 1.24% by mass.
items.why: The organics and water-bearing minerals found in Bennu are really Bennu's, not the spacecraft's.
points: An audit found the Bennu sample essentially free of contamination.
69 authors checked 121.6 grams; one isolated 1.24% by mass excepted.
Bennu's organics and water-bearing minerals really come from Bennu.

items.title: Terminal Instability of the Solar System Triggered by Stochastic Solar Mass Loss
items.hook: The Sun's death throes may scatter the outer planets
items.body: Standard models treat the Sun's late-life mass loss as smooth. Batygin, Fuller and Adams model it as discrete, stochastic events instead, which kick the planets' orbits. In ~40% of their simulated realizations, orbit crossings begin while the Sun is still on the red giant branch — before it becomes a white dwarf.
items.why: It shortens the expected stability lifetime of the outer Solar System by a large margin.
points: The dying Sun's mass loss may destabilise the outer planets.
Orbits crossed during the red giant phase in ~40% of simulations.
The outer Solar System may stay stable for far less time.

items.title: High Water D/H Ratio of Interstellar Object 3I/ATLAS
items.hook: 3I/ATLAS's odd water points to a metal-poor birthplace
items.body: The interstellar object 3I/ATLAS shows an unusually high deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio in its water. Astrochemical modeling asks what kind of nursery could produce that, and finds the observed ratio is most readily reproduced at subsolar metallicities.
items.why: Water chemistry may work as a fingerprint of the cloud a visiting object formed in.

jargon.metallicity: how much non-hydrogen a cloud holds

points: Interstellar object 3I/ATLAS has unusually deuterium-rich water.
Modeling best reproduces this ratio at subsolar metallicities.
Water chemistry may fingerprint where visiting objects were born.

items.title: Detection of hydrocarbons in Titan using high-resolution cross-correlation spectroscopy
items.hook: First cross-correlation detection of ethane at Titan
items.body: A team adapted high-resolution cross-correlation spectroscopy — a technique built for exoplanet atmospheres — and pointed it at Titan. They report the first HRCCS detection of ethane (C₂H₆), at a peak signal-to-noise of 5.17 ± 0.07, using cross-section-based templates.
items.why: If the method works on a moon we can check against, it can be trusted on atmospheres we can only observe from far away.

jargon.HRCCS: matching a spectrum against a template

points: An exoplanet technique detected ethane in Titan's atmosphere.
High-resolution cross-correlation spectroscopy reached signal-to-noise of 5.17.
Validating it on Titan builds trust for distant exoplanet atmospheres.

items.title: Steepening Optical Slopes in Exoplanet Transmission Spectra with Charged Hazes
items.hook: Electrically charged haze steepens exoplanet spectra
items.body: A microphysical model adds electric charge to haze particles in exoplanet atmospheres. Charged grains repel each other, which suppresses coagulation and keeps particle radii small. Charged, scattering-dominated hazes can then produce super-Rayleigh optical slopes even when vertical mixing is weak.
items.why: A slope astronomers usually read as strong mixing might instead report an atmosphere's electrical state.

jargon.coagulation: small particles sticking into bigger ones

points: Modeling suggests electric charge changes exoplanet haze behaviour.
Charged grains repel, stay small, and give steep super-Rayleigh slopes.
Steep slopes might reflect electrical state, not strong mixing.

items.title: The Atomic C/O Ratio of KELT-9b
items.hook: KELT-9b's carbon-to-oxygen ratio measured at 0.20
items.body: KELT-9b is the hottest known giant exoplanet — hot enough that molecules break apart into individual atoms. High-resolution spectroscopy of those atoms gives an atmospheric C/O ratio of 0.20 (+0.13 / −0.07), slightly below its host star's value.
items.why: C/O ratios are the main clue to where in its disk a planet formed before migrating inward.
points: Astronomers measured the hottest known giant exoplanet's C/O ratio.
C/O is 0.20, slightly below its host star's value.
C/O ratios hint where in its disk a planet formed.

items.title: JWST/MIRI Imaging Search for Kinematically Detected Protoplanetary Candidates
items.hook: JWST looked for kinematic protoplanets and saw none
items.body: Disk kinematics — wiggles in the gas motion of protoplanetary disks — have been used to infer embedded planets. A JWST/MIRI imaging campaign targeted those candidates directly and detected nothing, setting upper mass limits of roughly 3–20 Jupiter masses at separations of a few hundred au.
items.why: A clean null result: either the planets are fainter than expected, or the kinematic signatures have another cause.

jargon.kinematic signature: an unexplained motion in disk gas

points: JWST found none of the planets inferred from disk gas motions.
MIRI imaging set upper limits of roughly 3–20 Jupiter masses.
Planets are fainter than expected, or the signatures mean something else.

items.title: Direct Four-Spacecraft Measurement of Reconnection Exhaust Thickness in the Solar Wind
items.hook: Four spacecraft measure a reconnection exhaust directly
items.body: NASA's Magnetospheric Multiscale flies four spacecraft in formation. Across four current-sheet crossings in the pristine solar wind, the team measured reconnection exhaust thickness directly rather than inferring it from one probe: 29–31 ion inertial lengths, with a nonparallel exhaust geometry.
items.why: It validates the single-spacecraft estimates most of the field's reconnection measurements rely on.

jargon.exhaust: the outflow jet from that snap

points: Four MMS spacecraft directly measured a magnetic reconnection exhaust.
Exhaust thickness was 29–31 ion inertial lengths across four crossings.
Validates the single-spacecraft estimates most reconnection studies rely on.

items.title: Bifurcations in the Heliosphere: Global-scale Coronal Pseudostreamer Evolution
items.hook: The heliospheric current sheet can split, then reunite
items.body: MHD simulations of coronal pseudostreamers show the Sun's current sheet flipping between one-sheet and two-sheet configurations. When the corona's dipole and quadrupole components are roughly equal in magnitude, the model oscillates between the two states on timescales of days to weeks.
items.why: The current sheet's shape sets where solar wind structures hit Earth — a splitting one complicates forecasts.
points: Simulations show the Sun's current sheet can split and rejoin.
Flips over days to weeks when dipole and quadrupole roughly match.
A splitting sheet complicates forecasts of solar wind reaching Earth.

items.title: KMT-2026-BLG-0083L: A Two-Jovian-Planet System Orbiting an M Dwarf
items.hook: Microlensing finds two cold giants around an M dwarf
items.body: A microlensing event resolves into a two-planet system around a small M-dwarf star, with planet-to-star mass ratios of 5.25×10⁻³ and 3.04×10⁻³. One planet sits near the host's snow line; the other is far beyond it.
items.why: Microlensing sees cold, wide planets transit surveys structurally cannot — and small stars were not expected to build two giants.

jargon.snow line: where water ice can condense in a disk
jargon.microlensing: a star's gravity briefly magnifying another

points: Microlensing revealed two cold giant planets around an M dwarf.
One sits near the snow line, the other far beyond it.
Small stars were not expected to build two giant planets.

items.title: Limits on a Host Star Around Saturn-Mass Free-Floating Planet KMT-2024-BLG-0792
items.hook: No host star found out to 90 au of a rogue planet
items.body: KMT-2024-BLG-0792 is a Saturn-mass free-floating planet candidate. High-resolution interferometry searched the neighbourhood for a star it might belong to and detected no luminous host out to a projected separation of 90 au, with upper mass limits near 0.5–0.6 solar masses.
items.why: Ruling out a host is how a candidate rogue planet becomes a real one.

jargon.free-floating planet: a planet bound to no star

points: No host star found near a Saturn-mass rogue planet candidate.
Interferometry ruled out luminous hosts out to 90 au.
Ruling out a host moves a candidate toward confirmed rogue planet.

items.hook: 14,767 papers on what we actually test models for
items.body: A systematic sweep of evaluation resources published between 2022 and 2026 maps what benchmarks have been asking of language models. The emphasis has shifted toward action, interaction and professional tasks — and the survey notes that AI now takes part in building and judging the tests it is measured by.
items.why: Benchmarks decide what the field optimises for, so a drift in benchmarks is a drift in the whole field.

jargon.benchmark: a fixed test used to compare models

points: A survey mapped what language model benchmarks have been testing.
Covers 14,767 papers on evaluation resources from 2022 to 2026.
Benchmarks shifted toward action and professional tasks, steering the field.

items.title: Characterizing Web Search by Conversational LLM Agents
items.hook: What chatbots actually type into a search box
items.body: The first study to compare how ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and DeepSeek search the web finds the agents use distinctly different querying strategies, and raises attribution concerns in the answers they ground on what they retrieve.
items.why: These agents are becoming the layer between people and the web, and nobody outside the labs could see what they were asking.

jargon.grounding: basing an answer on retrieved sources

points: First comparison of how ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and DeepSeek search.
Each agent uses a distinctly different web querying strategy.
Raises attribution concerns as agents mediate people's access to the web.

items.title: BioPhys-Bridge: A Benchmark for Interdisciplinary Scientific Reasoning in Physics-Grounded Biological Research
items.hook: A 500-case test of reasoning across physics and biology
items.body: The benchmark asks models to do what an interdisciplinary researcher does: ground an observation in evidence, interpret it through a quantitative physics model, and connect it back to a biological mechanism. 500 cases drawn from biophysics literature.
items.why: Most benchmarks stay inside one field; the hard part of real research is crossing between them.

jargon.biophysics: physics methods applied to living systems

points: A new benchmark tests AI reasoning across physics and biology.
500 cases drawn from biophysics literature, linking evidence and models.
Real research requires crossing fields, which most benchmarks skip.

Internal Structure of Exotic Hadron Candidate f_0(980) by Using Fragmentation Functions
items.hook: A particle that changes what it is depending on how hard you look
items.body: The f0(980) has never fitted neatly into the quark model. Analysing it through fragmentation functions suggests it behaves like a four-quark state — a bound pair of kaons — at low energy, and like an ordinary quark-antiquark hadron at high energy.
items.why: Whether exotic hadrons are real states or loose molecules is one of the open questions in the field.

jargon.tetraquark: a hadron made of four quarks
jargon.fragmentation function: how a quark turns into hadrons

points: The f0(980) particle may change nature depending on energy scale.
Fragmentation functions suggest four-quark at low energy, ordinary at high.
Bears on whether exotic hadrons are real states or loose molecules.

Modulating task-outcome value to mitigate real-world procrastination via noninvasive brain stimulation
items.hook: Brain stimulation curbed procrastination in a double-blind trial
items.body: In a double-blind trial, noninvasive brain stimulation led to a lasting drop in how much people procrastinated in everyday life. The effect appeared to work by making future rewards feel more valuable, not by making the tasks themselves feel less unpleasant.
items.why: It points to a specific decision-making mechanism behind procrastination that could be targeted.

points: Noninvasive brain stimulation lastingly reduced everyday procrastination.
Double-blind trial; future rewards felt more valuable, tasks no less unpleasant.

items.title: Larger language models better align with neural representations of natural language
items.hook: Bigger language models predict brain activity better
items.body: The study compared language models of different sizes with recorded neural activity during language processing. Larger models captured the structure of language better and predicted brain responses more accurately, with gains that grew roughly logarithmically with model size.
items.why: It links AI scaling to how well models mirror the brain's handling of language.
items.image_credit: Figure: Zhuoqiao Hong et al., CC BY 4.0
points: Larger language models predicted recorded brain activity more accurately.
Gains grew roughly logarithmically with model size.
Links AI scaling to how well models mirror brain language processing.

items.title: Synergistic inhibition of Notch signaling and forced cell cycle re-entry drive Müller glia reprogramming in uninjured mouse retina
items.hook: Coaxing retinal support cells into becoming neurons in mice
items.body: Researchers combined blocking Notch signalling with pushing Müller glia back into the cell cycle in healthy mouse retinas. Together, the two interventions substantially increased the conversion of these glial cells into several types of retinal neurons.
items.why: Turning resident glia into neurons is a potential route to repairing vision loss.
items.image_credit: Figure: Baoshan Liao et al., CC BY 4.0
points: Retinal Müller glia were coaxed into becoming neurons in mice.
Combined Notch blocking with pushing glia back into the cell cycle.
A potential route to repairing vision loss.

items.title: Linear antibody epitope prediction using AlphaFold2
items.hook: AlphaFold2 repurposed to find where antibodies bind
items.body: The authors built PAbFold, a tool that uses AlphaFold2 to predict linear antibody epitopes from only the antibody and target protein sequences. It identifies binding sites accurately and quickly.
items.why: Faster epitope mapping could speed antibody development and characterisation.
items.image_credit: Figure: DeRoo et al., CC BY 4.0
points: PAbFold uses AlphaFold2 to predict where antibodies bind.
Needs only antibody and target protein sequences to find linear epitopes.
Faster epitope mapping could speed antibody development.

items.title: Screening the MMV Pathogen Box reveals the mitochondrial bc1-complex as a drug target in mature Toxoplasma gondii bradyzoites
items.hook: A weak spot in the dormant stage of Toxoplasma
items.body: Screening a compound library against mature, dormant-stage Toxoplasma gondii (bradyzoites) showed that these parasites depend on mitochondrial ATP production. The mitochondrial bc1 complex emerged as a promising drug target.
items.why: Chronic Toxoplasma infections currently have no cure, so a target in the dormant stage matters.
items.image_credit: Figure: Deborah Maus et al., CC BY 4.0
points: Dormant Toxoplasma parasites depend on mitochondrial ATP production.
A compound screen flagged the mitochondrial bc1 complex as target.
Chronic Toxoplasma infections currently have no cure.

items.title: Defective neuronal differentiation in Lowe syndrome is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired cilia-related Sonic Hedgehog signaling
items.hook: Mitochondrial faults linked to brain development in Lowe syndrome
items.body: Loss of the OCRL gene, which causes Lowe syndrome, produced mitochondrial dysfunction consistently across species. This was tied to altered neural differentiation and weaker Sonic Hedgehog signalling via cilia.
items.why: It suggests mechanisms behind the neurological symptoms of a rare genetic disease.
items.image_credit: Figure: Walkiewicz et al., CC BY 4.0
points: Losing the Lowe syndrome gene OCRL disrupted mitochondria across species.
Linked to altered neural differentiation and weaker cilia-based Hedgehog signalling.
Suggests mechanisms behind the disease's neurological symptoms.

items.title: An applicable and efficient retrograde monosynaptic circuit mapping tool for larval zebrafish
items.hook: New tool traces neural wiring in baby zebrafish
items.body: The study presents a retrograde monosynaptic tracing method for larval zebrafish that labels up to about 20 input neurons per starter cell. It does so with low toxicity to the labelled cells.
items.why: It gives a widely used model animal a practical way to map which neurons connect to which.
items.image_credit: Figure: Chen et al., CC BY 4.0
points: A new method traces neural connections in larval zebrafish.
Labels up to about 20 input neurons per starter cell, low toxicity.
Helps map which neurons connect in a widely used model animal.

items.title: DGKα and ζ deficiency causes regulatory T-cell dysregulation, destabilization, and conversion to pathogenic T-follicular helper cells to trigger IgG1-predominant autoimmunity
items.hook: Losing two enzymes turns immune peacekeepers into troublemakers
items.body: Diacylglycerol kinases alpha and zeta turned out to be essential for keeping regulatory T cells stable and for suppressing inflammatory programs. Without them, these cells destabilised, converted into pathogenic T-follicular helper cells and triggered autoimmunity.
items.why: It identifies a pathway that keeps immune tolerance in check and could inform autoimmune therapies.
items.image_credit: Figure: Lei Li et al., CC BY 4.0
points: Two enzymes keep regulatory T cells stable and anti-inflammatory.
Without DGK alpha and zeta, cells turned pathogenic and caused autoimmunity.
Could inform therapies for autoimmune disease.

items.title: Regional signaling controls stem cell-mediated regeneration in an invertebrate chordate
items.hook: Where you cut decides whether a sea squirt regrows
items.body: In the sea squirt Ciona robusta, lower body fragments regenerated but upper fragments did not. The difference came from region-specific signals controlling stem cell activation, not simply how many stem cells were present.
items.why: It shows local signalling, not just stem cell supply, limits regeneration in a close relative of vertebrates.
points: Only lower body fragments of the sea squirt Ciona regenerated.
Region-specific signals, not stem cell numbers, controlled stem cell activation.
Local signalling limits regeneration in a close vertebrate relative.

items.title: Collagen I promotes cancer cell survival via amino acid import and mTORC1/S6 activation
items.hook: Tumour scaffolding protein helps starving cancer cells survive
items.body: Collagen I in the tumour microenvironment helped cancer cells survive via integrin-dependent signalling that boosted amino acid import and mTORC1/S6 activity. The LAT1-4F2hc amino acid transporter was identified as a possible therapeutic target in nutrient-poor tumours.
items.why: It points to a druggable way tumours cope with nutrient scarcity.
points: Collagen I helps cancer cells survive when nutrients are scarce.
Integrin signalling boosted amino acid import and mTORC1/S6 activity.
The LAT1-4F2hc transporter may be a druggable target.

items.title: An engineered bacterial symbiont maps micron-scale sugar gradients in the honeybee gut
items.hook: Engineered gut bacterium maps sugar inside honeybees
items.body: Researchers engineered the honeybee gut symbiont Snodgrassella alvi into a biosensor that reports sugar levels. It revealed micron-scale nutrient gradients inside the living bee gut.
items.why: It provides a genetically tractable platform for sensing chemistry inside a living host.
items.image_credit: Figure: Chhun et al., CC BY 4.0
points: A honeybee gut bacterium was engineered into a sugar biosensor.
Engineered Snodgrassella alvi revealed micron-scale nutrient gradients in the gut.
Offers a platform for sensing chemistry inside living hosts.

items.title: Cyclic tri-adenylate controls a CARF-TM effector in type II Panoptes anti-phage systems
items.hook: How bacteria shut down when viruses strike
items.body: The study examines type II Panoptes, a bacterial defence system that relies on cyclic nucleotide signalling. When triggered, its membrane effector disrupts the cell membrane and halts growth, stopping phage infection.
items.why: Bacterial immune systems are a rich source of new molecular tools and insights into host-virus arms races.
points: Bacteria use the Panoptes system to stop virus infections.
Its membrane effector disrupts the cell membrane and halts growth.
Bacterial immune systems are a rich source of molecular tools.

items.title: R1-32-like public antibodies acquire tolerance to SARS-CoV-2 antigenic drift through somatic hypermutation
items.hook: Common antibodies evolve to keep up with COVID variants
items.body: A class of antibodies found in many people can mutate to tolerate changes in SARS-CoV-2 variants. The researchers identified an ultrapotent human R1-32-like antibody active against a broad range of variants.
items.why: Understanding how broad protection arises can guide vaccine and antibody design.
items.image_credit: Figure: Chuanying Niu et al., CC BY 4.0
points: Common antibodies can mutate to keep up with COVID variants.
Researchers found an ultrapotent R1-32-like antibody with broad activity.
Could guide vaccine and antibody design.

items.title: Atlastin-2-mediated endoplasmic reticulum membrane tethering is critical for flavivirus replication
items.hook: Dengue and Zika hijack a host membrane protein to replicate
items.body: The host protein atlastin-2 tethers endoplasmic reticulum membranes in a way that dengue and Zika viruses rely on. Depleting it disrupted the spatial distribution of viral replication organelles and reduced virus production.
items.why: Host factors like this are candidate targets for broad antiviral drugs.
points: Dengue and Zika rely on host protein atlastin-2 to replicate.
Depleting it disrupted replication organelles and reduced virus production.
Host factors like this could be broad antiviral drug targets.

items.title: Recurrent synapses between CO₂-sensitive olfactory sensory neurons enable robust CO₂ detection in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes
items.hook: Mosquito CO2 sensors amplify each other to find hosts
items.body: Connectome mapping showed that CO2-responsive sensory neurons in Aedes aegypti have more recurrent connections to one another than other sensory neuron types. This feedback supports amplified CO2 detection used in host seeking.
items.why: It helps explain how mosquitoes reliably find people, a key step in disease transmission.
items.image_credit: Figure: Bao et al., CC BY 4.0
points: Mosquito CO2-sensing neurons are wired to amplify each other.
Connectome mapping showed extra recurrent connections among CO2 neurons.
Explains how mosquitoes find people, a key step in disease spread.

items.title: Brain structural and functional connectivity converge prenatally but diverge after birth
items.hook: Brain wiring and activity patterns part ways after birth
items.body: Neuroimaging across development showed that structural and functional brain connectivity become more aligned before birth. After birth, through infancy and toddlerhood, that coupling shifted toward weakening.
items.why: It maps a basic transition in how the developing brain organises itself.
points: Brain structure and activity grow more aligned before birth.
After birth, through toddlerhood, that coupling shifted toward weakening.
Maps a basic transition in how the developing brain organises.

items.title: Machine learning–driven decoding of maternal immune signatures in repeated pregnancy loss
items.hook: Machine learning points to T cells in recurrent miscarriage
items.body: Machine learning applied to single-cell RNA data from uterine tissue of patients with repeated pregnancy loss found maternal T cells carried the most distinct and generalisable disease signatures. CXCR4 and JUN were nominated as druggable candidates.
items.why: It narrows down which immune cells and molecules to study for a poorly understood condition.
points: Machine learning implicates maternal T cells in recurrent miscarriage.
Single-cell RNA data nominated CXCR4 and JUN as druggable candidates.
Narrows which cells and molecules to study for this condition.

items.title: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances and kidney disease: Genetic associations and computational prioritization of candidate toxicogenomic pathways
items.hook: Forever chemicals show mixed genetic links to kidney disease
items.body: Using Mendelian randomization, genetically predicted higher PFOA levels were associated with lower risk of IgA nephropathy but higher risk of hypertensive nephropathy. Computational analysis prioritised CTNNB1, TP53 and EGFR among candidate pathways.
items.why: It sharpens questions about how PFAS exposure may affect kidney health.
points: PFOA showed mixed genetic links to different kidney diseases.
Mendelian randomization: lower IgA nephropathy risk, higher hypertensive nephropathy risk.
Sharpens questions about how PFAS may affect kidney health.

items.title: SmartHisto: Bayesian active learning for histology images
items.hook: Smarter labelling cuts expert effort for pathology AI
items.body: SmartHisto uses Bayesian active learning to pick the most informative regions within histology images for experts to label, instead of whole images. It reached a mean IoU of 0.75, outperforming competing approaches.
items.why: Expert annotation is a major bottleneck for medical image AI.
items.image_credit: Figure: Vijendran et al., CC BY 4.0
points: SmartHisto cuts how much experts must label for pathology AI.
Bayesian active learning picks regions; reached mean IoU of 0.75.
Expert annotation is a major bottleneck for medical image AI.

items.title: A practical risk framework for large language model use in life science research
items.hook: A practical guide to using LLMs safely in biology labs
items.body: The paper explains how LLM architecture yields both strong capabilities and typical failures such as hallucination and sycophancy. It offers a risk framework for life science workflows, with six supplementary guides containing worked examples and checklists.
items.why: Researchers increasingly rely on LLMs and need concrete ways to manage their errors.
items.image_credit: Figure: Thomas Sharpton et al., CC BY 4.0
points: A guide explains how to use LLMs safely in biology labs.
Risk framework plus six guides with worked examples and checklists.
Helps researchers manage errors like hallucination and sycophancy.

items.title: Hierarchical feature binding in a spiking neural network model of the primate ventral visual pathway
items.hook: Spiking network model shows how vision binds shape features
items.body: A spiking neural network modelled on the primate ventral visual pathway self-organised so that individual neurons responded to specific shape features. It produced repeating spatiotemporal firing patterns, some forming circuits that encode hierarchical relationships between features.
items.why: It offers a mechanistic account of the long-standing feature-binding problem in vision.
points: A spiking network model learned neurons tuned to shape features.
Modelled on the primate ventral pathway; showed repeating firing patterns.
Offers a mechanistic account of vision's feature-binding problem.

items.title: Multiscale computational modeling to quantify how spiral artery remodeling alters wall shear stress on placental villi
items.hook: Simulations link faulty artery remodelling to placental damage
items.body: Multiscale models of placental blood flow showed that incomplete remodelling of spiral arteries sharply increases shear stress on placental villi. The stresses reached levels consistent with tissue loss and placental lake formation.
items.why: It identifies shear-stress thresholds relevant to pregnancy complications.
points: Models link faulty spiral artery remodelling to placental damage.
Incomplete remodelling sharply raised shear stress on placental villi.
Identifies shear-stress thresholds relevant to pregnancy complications.

items.title: High-throughput virus quantification using cytopathic effect area analysis
items.hook: Automated image analysis counts virus infectivity at scale
items.body: The authors developed an assay that quantifies virus infectivity by measuring the area of cell damage in images, suited to high-throughput screening. An nnU-Net model matched manual thresholding closely.
items.why: It could replace slower traditional infectivity assays in antiviral screening.
points: An image-based assay measures virus infectivity at high throughput.
An nnU-Net model measuring cell damage matched manual thresholding closely.
Could replace slower infectivity assays in antiviral screening.

items.title: Monte Carlo modeling of the formation and organization of ion channel clustering
items.hook: Simulations reveal a sweet spot for ion channel clustering
items.body: Monte Carlo simulations of ion channel organisation found a biphasic link between interaction energy and cluster size, with the largest clusters at intermediate interaction strengths. Systems with several channel types formed hierarchical clusters.
items.why: Channel clustering shapes electrical signalling in neurons and heart cells.
points: Ion channels cluster most at intermediate interaction strengths.
Monte Carlo simulations; multiple channel types formed hierarchical clusters.
Clustering shapes electrical signalling in neurons and heart cells.

NASA's Hubble Spots an Out-of-Sync Galaxy
items.hook: This galaxy's core spins at right angles to the rest of it
items.body: A new Hubble image shows NGC 4698, a spiral galaxy about 55 million light-years away in the Virgo Cluster. Its central stars and gas rotate perpendicular to the outer disk, and its bulge also sticks out at a right angle. Astronomers think the galaxy picked up gas from outside, possibly in a minor merger.
items.why: Mismatched rotation keeps a record of a galaxy's past collisions and feeding.
items.image_credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, D. Thilker, the MAUVE-HST Team (CC BY 4.0)
points: Hubble shows galaxy NGC 4698's core spinning perpendicular to its disk.
Spiral galaxy about 55 million light-years away in Virgo Cluster.
Likely picked up outside gas, possibly in a minor merger.

items.title: Photo Release: Webb reveals stunning panorama of star formation
items.hook: Webb finds the lightest free-floating brown dwarfs yet
items.body: Webb has made one of its largest images, showing the young star cluster IC 348, about 1,000 light-years away in Perseus. Follow-up NIRSpec spectra found brown dwarfs as light as about twice Jupiter's mass, the least massive known. One of them appears to have a disc around it, so planets could form around such a tiny object.
items.why: It tests how small an object can be and still form the way a star does.
items.image_credit: ESA/Webb, NASA, CSA, K. Luhman, C. Alves De Oliveira, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb) (CC BY 4.0)
points: Webb found the least massive known free-floating brown dwarfs.
As light as about twice Jupiter's mass, in cluster IC 348.
One has a disc, so planets could form around it.

items.title: Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn's south pole
items.hook: Saturn's south pole now has a ten-sided jet stream
items.body: Hubble images from 2023 onward, taken for the OPAL outer-planets programme, show a ten-sided wave pattern circling Saturn's south pole. It is the first large regular polygon seen in the southern hemisphere and is related to, but different from, the famous hexagon in the north. Cassini saw no such pattern while it orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, which suggests the decagon is new.
items.why: A pattern forming in real time lets scientists test how giant-planet jet streams organise themselves.
items.image_credit: NASA, ESA, STScI, A. Sánchez-Lavega (University of the Basque Country), A. Simon (NASA-GSFC), M. Wong (UC Berkeley); Image Processing: A. Pagan (STScI) (CC BY 4.0)
points: Hubble spotted a ten-sided jet stream around Saturn's south pole.
Cassini saw no such pattern from 2004 to 2017, suggesting it's new.
A forming pattern lets scientists test how jet streams organise.

items.title: Milky Way's fastest star orbits our supermassive black hole so closely it feels its spin
items.hook: A star moving at 8% of light speed circles our black hole
items.body: Using the GRAVITY+ instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope Interferometer, astronomers found S301, the fastest known star in the Milky Way. It orbits Sagittarius A* every 8.7 years and reaches about 25,000 km/s at closest approach, roughly 12 times the Earth–Sun distance from the black hole. It passes close enough that the black hole's spin affects its orbit.
items.why: Stars this close are a way to measure how a black hole spins and to test general relativity.
points: Star S301, the Milky Way's fastest known, orbits our black hole.
Reaches about 25,000 km/s, orbiting Sagittarius A* every 8.7 years.
Could measure the black hole's spin and test general relativity.

items.title: Hubble solves merger mystery from Milky Way's early years
items.hook: The young Milky Way swallowed a dwarf galaxy 11.8 billion years ago
items.body: Astronomers measured the ages and metal content of 39 globular clusters in the inner Milky Way with Hubble and compared them with Gaia data. They found a separate group of clusters left over from a dwarf galaxy nicknamed Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles, which merged with our galaxy about 11.8 billion years ago. The result, published in Nature Astronomy, takes the Milky Way's known merger history 1.8 billion years further back.
items.why: It shows how our galaxy was assembled from smaller pieces in its first few billion years.
points: The Milky Way absorbed a dwarf galaxy 11.8 billion years ago.
Hubble and Gaia data on 39 globular clusters revealed its remnants.
Extends our galaxy's known merger history 1.8 billion years further back.

items.title: Science Release: Webb reveals dust and water surviving in the extreme environment around the Milky Way's central black hole
items.hook: Dust and water survive next to our galaxy's black hole
items.body: Webb's MIRI instrument detected silicate dust and water around IRS 3, an evolved star only about 0.55 light-years from Sagittarius A*. The star is about six times the Sun's mass, is losing mass quickly, and is wrapped in a dusty envelope roughly 10,000 astronomical units across. The study, in Astronomy & Astrophysics, shows that dust can form even in the harsh radiation near a supermassive black hole.
items.why: It changes what we think galactic centres can make and keep.
items.image_credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, F. Peißker, J. Lu, F. Yusef-Zadeh, N. B. Sabha, C. Chan (CC BY 4.0)
points: Webb found dust and water around a star near Sagittarius A*.
Star IRS 3 sits only about 0.55 light-years from the black hole.
Dust can form even in harsh radiation near supermassive black holes.

items.title: Photo Release: Lion Nebula roars to life for Webb
items.hook: Webb's infrared view of the dying star behind the 'Lion Nebula'
items.body: Webb imaged the planetary nebula NGC 2392, nicknamed the Lion Nebula, with its NIRCam and MIRI cameras. The image shows the shells and rings of gas thrown off by a dying star, now a white dwarf. It also shows compact dust clumps with comet-like tails, lit by the hot white dwarf.
items.why: Planetary nebulae show the Sun's likely fate in detail.
items.image_credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI. Image Processing: A. Pagan (STScI) (CC BY 4.0)
points: Webb imaged the Lion Nebula, a dying star's cast-off gas.
NIRCam and MIRI show shells, rings and comet-tailed dust clumps.
Planetary nebulae show the Sun's likely fate in detail.

items.title: Astronomers find strongest evidence yet that Betelgeuse has a companion
items.hook: Betelgeuse's hidden companion star finally photographed
items.body: Using the SPHERE instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, a team led by Miguel Montargès directly imaged a companion star next to the red supergiant Betelgeuse. Observations were timed for when the companion was predicted to be farthest from the star. It turned out to be about two to three times the Sun's mass, heavier and brighter than expected.
items.why: It ends a search for a companion that went on for about a century.
points: Betelgeuse's companion star was directly imaged for the first time.
VLT's SPHERE found it about two to three times the Sun's mass.
Ends a search for the companion lasting about a century.

items.title: New 'exomoon' detection challenges cosmic labels
items.hook: Possible 'moon' found circling a brown dwarf
items.body: Using the CRIRES+ spectrograph on ESO's Very Large Telescope, astronomers measured a tiny wobble in a brown dwarf in the CD-35 2722 system, caused by an object at least as massive as Jupiter orbiting it. The brown dwarf itself is over 30 times Jupiter's mass and orbits a star of about half the Sun's mass. If confirmed, the object could count as the first moon found outside the Solar System, but it does not orbit a planet, which makes it hard to label.
items.why: It blurs the line between planets, moons and failed stars.
points: A possible moon was found orbiting a brown dwarf.
CRIRES+ detected a wobble from an object at least Jupiter-mass.
If confirmed, it blurs lines between planets, moons and failed stars.

items.title: NASA Invites Media to Albania Artemis Accords Signing Ceremony
items.hook: Albania becomes the 73rd Artemis Accords signatory
items.body: Albania is set to sign the Artemis Accords at NASA Headquarters in Washington on 21 September 2026. That makes it the 73rd country to join the US-led principles for peaceful civil exploration of the Moon and beyond. NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson is hosting Albania's foreign minister, Ferit Hoxha.
items.why: The Accords keep growing as a shared set of rules for lunar activity.

It becomes the 73rd country to join the US-led principles.
The Accords keep growing as shared rules for lunar activity.

Superconductivity in Monolayer-Trilayer Phase of La₃Ni₂O₇ under High Pressure
items.hook: Nickelate superconductor needs its paired layers to hit 80 K
items.body: Researchers squeezed a variant of the nickel oxide La3Ni2O7 in which single and triple layers alternate (the '1313' structure). Under high pressure it superconducts only up to about 3.6 K, far below the roughly 80 K reached by the version built from paired layers. The comparison indicates that coupled bilayers are what make high-temperature superconductivity possible in this material.
items.why: Pinning down which structural ingredient drives nickelate superconductivity narrows the search for new high-temperature superconductors.
points: A layered nickelate variant superconducts only up to about 3.6 K.
Paired-layer version reaches roughly 80 K under high pressure.
Suggests coupled bilayers drive high-temperature superconductivity in this material.

items.title: Enduring Mechanical Memory from the Constitutive Response of Elastically Recoverable Nanostructured Materials
items.hook: Carbon nanotube foam remembers how it was squeezed
items.body: Foams made of vertically aligned carbon nanotubes show 'return point memory': after being compressed and released, they return to earlier mechanical states along the same path. The authors link this lasting memory to how the elastically recovering nanostructure responds to load.
items.why: Materials that store information in their mechanical response could enable mechanical computing and new shock-absorbing designs.
points: Carbon nanotube foams show 'return point memory' of past compression.
They return to earlier mechanical states along the same path.
Could enable mechanical computing and new shock-absorbing designs.

items.title: Emergent Altermagnetism at Surfaces of Antiferromagnets: Full Symmetry Classification and Material Identification
items.hook: Ordinary antiferromagnets can hide a new magnetism on their surfaces
items.body: Using a symmetry framework built for surfaces, theorists show that the broken symmetry at the surface of conventional antiferromagnets can turn the surface layer into a two-dimensional altermagnet. They classify the possibilities and identify more than 150 candidate materials.
items.why: Altermagnets are a recently recognised magnetic class of interest for spintronics, and this greatly widens where they might be found.
points: Antiferromagnet surfaces could host two-dimensional altermagnetism, theory shows.
A surface symmetry framework identifies more than 150 candidate materials.
Widens where altermagnets, of interest for spintronics, might be found.

items.title: Quantum Birthmarks: Ergodicity Breaking Beyond Scarring
items.hook: Chaotic quantum systems never fully forget where they started
items.body: Theorists describe 'quantum birthmarks': a lasting imprint of a quantum system's initial state and its early dynamics that persists instead of washing out. The effect goes beyond previously known 'quantum scars' and runs against the classical expectation that chaotic systems lose memory of their start.
items.why: It challenges the assumption that chaotic quantum systems fully thermalise, with consequences for statistical physics and quantum technologies.
points: Theorists describe 'quantum birthmarks' in chaotic quantum systems.
An imprint of the initial state persists, beyond known quantum scars.
Challenges the assumption that chaotic quantum systems fully thermalise.

items.title: Production and Decay Dynamics of the Charmed Baryon Λc⁺ in e⁺e⁻ Annihilations near Threshold
items.hook: BESIII sees charmed baryons produced with a spin tilt
items.body: The BESIII collaboration studied Lambda-c+ baryons, which contain a charm quark, created in electron-positron collisions just above the energy needed to make them. They observed that the baryons are produced with transverse polarization, a preferred spin direction.
items.why: Spin measurements near threshold test how the strong force produces heavy baryons and help probe their decays.
points: BESIII found charmed Lambda-c+ baryons produced with a spin tilt.
Made in electron-positron collisions just above the production threshold.
Tests how the strong force produces heavy baryons.

items.title: Overcoming Intrinsic Material Limitations through Cavity Feedback
items.hook: Feedback loop beats magnetic losses to link light, spin and sound
items.body: In a cavity magnomechanics setup, the team used an active feedback loop to control dissipation and counter the material's built-in magnetic losses. This let them reach strong coupling among microwave photons, magnons (spin waves) and phonons (vibrations).
items.why: Engineering around material losses opens routes to hybrid quantum devices that convert signals between different carriers.
points: Feedback control linked microwave photons, magnons and phonons strongly.
An active feedback loop countered the material's built-in magnetic losses.
Opens routes to hybrid quantum devices converting between signal carriers.

items.title: Pomeranchuk Instability Induced by an Emergent Higher-Order Van Hove Singularity on the Distorted Kagome Surface of Co₃Sn₂S₂
items.hook: Warped kagome surface makes electrons pick a direction
items.body: On the surface of the kagome magnet Co3Sn2S2, a lattice distortion flattens saddle points in the electronic structure into a higher-order Van Hove singularity. This triggers a d-wave Pomeranchuk instability, in which the electron Fermi surface spontaneously deforms and nematic, direction-dependent states appear.
items.why: It shows how surface distortion can tune electron correlations in kagome materials, a hot platform for exotic quantum phases.
points: A distorted kagome magnet surface makes electrons prefer one direction.
Distortion on Co3Sn2S2 creates a higher-order Van Hove singularity.
Surface distortion can tune electron correlations in kagome materials.

items.title: Spatial structure of multipartite entanglement at measurement induced phase transitions
items.hook: Measured quantum circuits hide long-range many-party entanglement
items.body: Measurement-induced phase transitions occur in quantum circuits mixing gates and measurements. The authors show these transitions carry long-range entanglement shared among many parties, described by a hierarchy of exponents, and compute the exponents exactly for a 1D model that maps onto percolation, with numerical checks and a 2D extension.
items.why: It clarifies how entanglement is organised in monitored quantum systems, relevant to quantum computing and error correction.
points: Measurement-induced transitions carry long-range entanglement shared among many parties.
Exponents computed exactly for a 1D model mapping onto percolation.
Clarifies entanglement in monitored systems, relevant to error correction.

items.title: Generalising Aumann's Agreement Theorem
items.hook: Quantum agents can't agree to disagree either
items.body: Aumann's theorem says rational agents with a common prior and common knowledge of each other's beliefs cannot end up disagreeing. The authors argue this holds in quantum theory and extend it to any generalised probability theory, concluding it follows from how new information is conditioned on.
items.why: It settles a debate on whether quantum physics allows reasoning that classical probability forbids.
points: Aumann's 'agreeing to disagree' theorem holds in quantum theory too.
Extended to any generalised probability theory via information conditioning.
Settles whether quantum physics allows reasoning classical probability forbids.

items.title: Streaming Belief Propagation on Mixed-Alphabet Tanner Graphs for Practical Quantum Memory
items.hook: Real-time decoder keeps pace with quantum error correction
items.body: The authors propose a streaming belief-propagation decoder that processes error syndromes continuously using a sliding space-time window. In simulations with realistic circuit noise it reached error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% across several topological codes.
items.why: Fast, continuous decoding is a practical bottleneck for keeping quantum memories alive.
points: A streaming decoder handles quantum error correction continuously.
Sliding-window belief propagation reached thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87%.
Fast decoding is a bottleneck for keeping quantum memories alive.

items.title: Quantum Simulation of Nuclear Dynamics in First Quantization
items.hook: Early fault-tolerant quantum computers could simulate nuclear reactions
items.body: This work estimates the full resources to simulate nuclear dynamics with a standard low-energy nuclear model on a quantum computer. Working in first quantization gives an exponential improvement over earlier approaches, and simple low-energy scattering might need tens of millions of T gates and a few hundred logical qubits.
items.why: Nuclear reaction rates matter for astrophysics and experiments but are classically very expensive to compute.
items.image_credit: Figure: Spagnoli et al., CC BY 4.0
points: Early fault-tolerant quantum computers could simulate nuclear reactions.
Tens of millions of T gates, a few hundred logical qubits.
Nuclear reaction rates are very expensive to compute classically.

items.title: A brief history of quantum vs classical computational advantage
items.hook: Every quantum advantage claim so far, and how it fared
items.body: This review surveys all experiments to date that claimed quantum computational advantage, along with loopholes and classical rebuttals that followed. It also covers theoretical advantage in problems such as optimisation and recent progress in quantum error correction.
items.why: It gives a clear scorecard for a field full of contested claims.
points: A review surveys every quantum advantage claim made so far.
Covers loopholes, classical rebuttals and error correction progress.
A clear scorecard for a field full of contested claims.

items.title: Checkerboard-type Zhang-Rice states in overdoped cuprate superconductors
items.hook: Overdoped cuprates reorganise their electrons into a checkerboard
items.body: Using optical spectroscopy on La2-xSrxCuO4 across a wide doping range (x = 0.15 to 0.60), with supporting quantum Monte Carlo simulations, the team found the electronic structure reconstructs strongly beyond x = 0.2. They propose a checkerboard arrangement of Zhang-Rice states that explains coexisting mobile and localised carriers.
items.why: The little-studied overdoped regime adds constraints on how cuprate high-temperature superconductivity works.
points: Overdoped cuprates' electronic structure reconstructs strongly beyond x = 0.2.
Optical spectroscopy on La2-xSrxCuO4 from x = 0.15 to 0.60.
Proposed checkerboard arrangement constrains how cuprate superconductivity works.

items.hook: An approved ataxia drug switches off a key inflammaging switch
items.body: A high-throughput screen found that omaveloxolone, already FDA-approved for Friedreich's ataxia, causes cells to destroy the immune-signalling protein STING. The drug wedges into STING and destabilises its shape, tagging it for breakdown by the proteasome. In aged male mice it lowered STING levels and eased age-related inflammation, though its known antioxidant (NRF2) effect probably contributes too.

items.hook: Blurrier microscope images can make AI segmentation better, not worse
items.body: Researchers retrained popular deep-learning segmentation models on microscopy images shrunk to between 6% and 50% of their original resolution. Lower resolution also means faster imaging, less storage and quicker inference.
items.why: Labs could image faster, with less light damage and far less data, without sacrificing AI analysis quality.

items.hook: Knocking out one protein slows deadly brain-tumour stem cells
items.body: Using stem cells taken from patients' glioblastomas, researchers found that the CSN1 subunit of the COP9 signalosome is needed for the cells to grow. Deleting CSN1 significantly extended survival in mice carrying these tumours. Without CSN1 the signalosome failed to assemble, cell-cycle programmes were disrupted, cell-death pathways switched on and AP-1 signalling via JNK and c-Jun dropped.
items.why: Glioblastoma has few effective treatments, and this identifies a new vulnerability in the stem cells thought to drive tumour regrowth.

items.title: Generative AI as a cognitive support tool in early-stage design ideation: A human–AI co-ideation experiment
items.hook: AI brainstorming helps design students frame problems, not innovate more
items.body: Thirty-two design students each brainstormed both with a text-and-image AI workflow and without it. Experts rated AI-assisted ideas higher on problem framing and mechanism, but human-only ideas higher on innovation and solution strategies. Students felt more supported with AI, yet that did not translate into better originality or design refinement.
items.why: It offers controlled evidence that generative AI shifts what kind of creative work improves rather than improving everything.

canon.why: Two networks trained against each other — the idea that made generated images convincing.

canon.title: Observation of a new particle in the search for the Standard Model Higgs boson
canon.why: The last missing piece of the Standard Model, found 48 years after it was predicted.

canon.title: A Programmable Dual-RNA–Guided DNA Endonuclease in Adaptive Bacterial Immunity
canon.who: Jinek, Chylinski, Fonfara, Hauer, Doudna and Charpentier
canon.why: CRISPR-Cas9 turned from a bacterial immune system into a tool for editing any genome.

canon.title: Suppression of RNA Recognition by Toll-like Receptors
canon.why: The modified-nucleoside trick that stops the body attacking mRNA. Ignored for years, then it made the COVID vaccines work.

canon.title: Observational Evidence from Supernovae for an Accelerating Universe
canon.why: The expansion is speeding up, and nobody knows why. Dark energy is the name for not knowing.

canon.title: Evidence for Oscillation of Atmospheric Neutrinos
canon.why: Neutrinos change type as they travel, which means they have mass — the Standard Model said they did not.

canon.title: LixCoO2: A new cathode material for batteries of high energy density
canon.why: The cathode inside the lithium-ion battery in your phone. A Nobel, 39 years later.

canon.title: A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s
canon.why: They thought it was pigeon droppings in the antenna. It was the afterglow of the Big Bang.

canon.title: Detailed Balance Limit of Efficiency of p-n Junction Solar Cells
canon.why: Why a single solar cell tops out near a third of the sunlight it catches — and why tandems exist.

canon.title: Experimental Test of Parity Conservation in Beta Decay
canon.why: Nature tells left from right. Physicists had assumed for decades that it could not.

canon.title: Synthesis of the Elements in Stars
canon.why: How every element heavier than helium got made. The paper that ties nuclear physics to the sky.

canon.title: Some Criteria for a Power Producing Thermonuclear Reactor
canon.why: How hot, how dense and for how long — the bar every fusion machine is still measured against.

canon.title: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid
canon.why: One page, and the double helix. Built on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data, which she was not told they had.

canon.title: Über den Nachweis und das Verhalten der bei der Bestrahlung des Urans mittels Neutronen entstehenden Erdalkalimetalle
canon.why: The chemistry showing uranium had split into barium. They could not explain it, and published anyway.

canon.title: Disintegration of Uranium by Neutrons: a New Type of Nuclear Reaction
canon.why: The explanation Hahn could not give, worked out over a winter walk. Meitner was left off the Nobel.

canon.title: A relation between distance and radial velocity among extra-galactic nebulae
canon.why: Two and a half pages showing the universe is expanding. Cosmology starts here.

watch.name: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
watch.why: Nine lectures building a working GPT from nothing, in code, with every line explained.

watch.name: Neural networks
watch.why: The visual explanation of what a network is actually doing. Start here if the maths looks opaque.

watch.name: Practical Deep Learning for Coders
watch.why: Top-down: you train a working model in lesson one and learn why it worked afterwards.

watch.name: Short courses (agents, RAG, evaluation)
watch.why: Short, current, built with the labs themselves — though the catalogue has moved to a membership.

watch.name: Paper walkthroughs
watch.why: Reads the week's papers out loud and argues with them, which is how you learn to read them yourself.

watch.name: PBS Space Time
watch.why: The rare channel that keeps the real equations in and still stays followable.

watch.name: Dr. Becky
watch.why: A working astrophysicist walking through the month's results, including the ones that did not hold up.

watch.name: Fermilab
watch.why: Particle physics explained by the lab that does it, without the press-release gloss.

watch.name: Cool Worlds
watch.why: A working exoplanet astronomer thinking out loud about habitability and how we would ever know.

watch.name: Anton Petrov
watch.why: A short, careful video on almost every new astronomy result, usually within days of the paper.

watch.name: Kurzgesagt
watch.why: The most beautiful science animation being made, and the sources are published alongside each video.

watch.name: Deep Sky Videos
watch.why: Real astronomers talking through objects one at a time, telescope time included.

watch.name: Event Horizon
watch.why: Long interviews with the researchers themselves — where cosmology arguments actually get made.

watch.name: Scott Manley
watch.why: Orbital mechanics and launch failures explained by someone who reads the telemetry.

watch.name: Astrum
watch.why: Built from real probe imagery — what the spacecraft actually sent back, not an artist's impression.

books.title: Bayesian Data Analysis
books.who: Gelman, Carlin, Stern, Dunson, Vehtari and Rubin
books.why: How to reason about uncertainty when you have a model and not much data. Free PDF from the authors.

books.title: Numerical Recipes
books.why: The algorithms behind the library functions you call, explained well enough to know when they will fail you.

books.title: Statistical Data Analysis
books.why: The standard reference for how physicists actually handle errors, fits and limits. Short, and nothing wasted.

books.title: Data Reduction and Error Analysis for the Physical Sciences
books.why: The first statistics book most physics students meet, and the one they keep going back to.

books.title: The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
books.why: If you are going to publish plots, read this before you publish more of them.

books.title: An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics
books.why: The standard undergraduate course in one very heavy volume — stars, galaxies, cosmology, all of it.

books.title: Introduction to Cosmology
books.why: The clearest first cosmology book there is. You can read it end to end without getting stuck.

books.title: Black Holes and Time Warps
books.why: Written before LIGO detected anything, by the person who argued it would. Worth reading for that alone.

books.title: The First Three Minutes
books.why: A Nobel laureate walking through the early universe minute by minute, without hiding the physics.

books.title: Liftoff
books.why: How SpaceX nearly died before Falcon 1 reached orbit. Reported, not mythologised.

books.title: Reentry
books.why: The sequel: Falcon 9, reuse, and the decisions that turned a survivor into the whole market.

books.title: Space Mission Analysis and Design
books.why: The engineering reference the industry actually sizes missions with. Known simply as SMAD.

books.title: The Right Stuff
books.why: Why anyone climbs onto a rocket at all. Still the best writing about test pilots and nerve.

books.title: Modern Particle Physics
books.why: The current standard course. Works the calculations through instead of quoting results.

books.title: Introduction to Elementary Particles
books.why: Griffiths explains things the way a good supervisor would. Start here before Thomson.

books.title: Review of Particle Physics
books.why: Every measured property of every known particle, updated yearly and free. The field's single most-used document.

books.title: Lost in Math
books.why: An argument that beauty has been a bad guide in theoretical physics. Contested, and worth arguing with.

books.title: Plasma Physics and Fusion Energy
books.why: What it would actually take to build a fusion reactor, with the engineering constraints left in.

books.title: The Making of the Atomic Bomb
books.why: A Pulitzer for a book that is also a genuine history of 20th-century nuclear physics. Read it for Meitner and Bohr.

books.title: Midnight in Chernobyl
books.why: Reactor physics as it behaves when institutions fail. The clearest account of what actually happened.

books.title: Deep Learning
books.why: The foundations, from linear algebra up. Free online, and still the reference for why things work.

books.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction
books.why: Bridges classical statistics and deep learning in one framework. Draft PDF free, code in Python and JAX.

books.title: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction
books.why: By the people who built the field. Free PDF, and still the clearest treatment of the basics.

books.title: The Alignment Problem
books.why: The honest version of why making these systems do what we meant is hard, told through the research.

books.title: Sustainable Energy — Without the Hot Air
books.why: Every energy argument turned into kilowatt-hours per person per day. Free online, and it settles a lot of arguments.

books.title: Molecular Biology of the Cell
books.why: The textbook of cell biology. If you come from physics, this is where the vocabulary comes from.

books.title: The Gene
books.why: From Mendel to gene editing, written by an oncologist with a family history that makes it personal.

books.title: The Code Breaker
books.why: Jennifer Doudna and the race to CRISPR, with the rivalries left in.

books.title: The Emperor of All Maladies
books.why: A biography of cancer. Won the Pulitzer, and explains why the mRNA cancer vaccines matter so much.
